A junked PDP-7, a family away and a new operating system
How iTunes, written in a week, sealed the case for Unix

brief.head: Second systems sink
brief.text: A first system is built by frail, terrified mavericks, Ajay Shah said. Success breeds arrogance, and the second system overreaches. Multics was the classic case. {032-C04}

brief.head: The man page leads
brief.text: Writing a good man page forces clear thinking about what a program should and should not do, Ajay Shah said, and invites others to attack it. {032-C11}

brief.head: Name your files well
brief.text: Lowercase for files, uppercase for directories, underscores for spaces, a README everywhere: Ajay Shah’s defence against a forgetful mind, with files thirty or forty years old. {032-C18}

brief.head: Impossible, they said
brief.text: Top research groups told the Aadhaar team that matching anyone against 1.4 billion records could not be done. “They wrote it themselves and they did it,” Ajay Shah said. {032-S12}

brief.head: Hamming’s prophecy
brief.text: Richard Hamming predicted in the early sixties that over half of Bell Labs’ work would be computation. Every sad graduate student now knows it, Ajay Shah said. {032-J04}

thought.text: Don’t play for 50 days, don’t play for 50 weeks, play for fifty years.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, on the devotion it takes to build code that lasts for decades

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s long-promised Unix episode, with Amit Varma
lead.head: Everything is Unix
body: In an earlier episode, Ajay Shah promised to do an episode on Unix if enough viewers asked for one. They did. Amit Varma introduced it as one of the great passions of Shah’s life and the driving force of much of his creativity.
Over two hours, the hosts argued that Unix is more than software. It is the story of a remarkable lab, and a philosophy that, as Varma put it, one could choose to reprogram oneself through.

And it runs nearly everything. Shah listed Android and iOS phones, the Kindle, the iPad, the servers behind Amazon and the cloud. Of the 500 most powerful computers in the world, he said, 490 or more run some variant of Unix.
“So there is really no other operating system other than Unix today,” he said. The one holdout is Microsoft, whose Windows machines are a declining share of the world.
## A special place

Varma began with Bell Labs, the research arm of AT&T where Unix was born. Its secret, Shah argued, was not money. Murray Hill had about 3,000 employees, around 1,000 of them PhDs, a scale many organisations, even in India, could afford today.
“So it’s not the magic of resourcing,” he said. “It is some other magic. It’s a magic of culture, it’s a magic of management.” {032-C01}

That culture gave Ken Thompson, back from the failed Multics project, the room to build Unix in three weeks on an obsolete computer nobody wanted, even though management had refused to fund operating-systems research. {032-S05}
From there, Shah traced the line through the C language, the universities and Berkeley to the internet, Linux and Apple.
## Why Unix won

Much of the conversation was about why. Shah’s first answer was aesthetic. Systems built from a few simple components, with many features thrown away, work better because the human mind can grasp them.
“So I want to use the idea that simplicity and beauty is the user interface of the human mind,” he said. {032-C08}
Build one small tool at a time, he said, make it bulletproof, and let people combine tools like Lego blocks. Write code as you would write prose. Share it, as scientists share their proofs.

Varma, who teaches a writing course, said that writing clearly forces you to think clearly, and asked whether programming does the same. “Good programmers become better thinkers,” Shah replied. “But it’s got to be done right.”
Shah also argued that Unix and the internet were built to allow anonymity and encryption, and so kept computing from becoming a straitjacket controlled by corporations or governments. {032-C16}
## The command line
Then Shah opened a terminal. In a screencast, he showed how to name files with care, sort a table of the show’s episodes and join commands with the pipe.
By the end, viewers had written a one-line awk program. Had they done something clever, or become programmers? “The answer is both,” Shah said.
“This is part of how the Unix world works that programming is for everybody.” {032-C20}

second.label: Talent spotting
second.head: A forgery that paid off
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the professor who bent the rules for Ken Thompson
body: As an undergraduate at UC Berkeley, Ken Thompson worked on the university computer from midnight to 8 a.m., when it was all his. When a professor asked whether he would go to graduate school, Thompson said no. He thought he was just a regular guy. {032-S03}
Without telling him, Ajay Shah said, the professor filled in the application, forged his signature and sent it in. Thompson was accepted.

Shah told a similar story about his father, who went back to education through night school and did not get good marks in his master’s at Bombay University. The department’s elders, who knew him, took him into the PhD anyway. In India today, Shah said, everything is regimented. {032-C05}

quote.text: We should always look at the person and not at mechanical procedure.

third.head: Don’t lose heart, Linus
body: In 1991 a young student in Finland posted on Net News that he had been fooling around with the code of Minix and had written a brand new operating system. What did people think? {032-S09}
The reply from Andy Tanenbaum, a great computer scientist, was “extremely mean and critical”, Ajay Shah said. Shah, older than Linus Torvalds, thought it unfair.
“So I wrote email to Linus saying you should not be disheartened. What you’re doing is very important,” Shah said.

He booted Linux when it reached version 0.1. Apart from seven or eight years on Mac OS X, it has been his only system since. Today, he said, the Linux kernel is managed by 10,000 or 20,000 programmers spread all over the world. {032-C17}
third.caption: his 1991 email to Linus Torvalds

p2.deck: History, philosophy and practice of the operating system that runs the world, as discussed by Ajay Shah and Amit Varma

sections.label: The place
sections.head: A factory for ideas
sections.caption: Bell Labs and its long game
body: Asked where he would go in a time machine, Bill Gates chose Bell Labs in December 1947, Amit Varma said: the month the transistor was created. {#gates}

By the sixties, AT&T’s research laboratory employed more than 15,000 people. Telephony was a natural monopoly, so AT&T had a guaranteed revenue stream and could fund work that need not pay off by the next quarter.
The numbers are often overstated, Varma said. About 2.8 per cent of revenues went to R&D, and 0.3 per cent to basic research. {#rd} What mattered, he said, was the long horizon. {032-S01}
## Eccentrics, not dreamers
It was, Varma said, “a place for eccentrics but not dreamers”. You could take the long view, but ideas had to become things. {032-C02}

Brian Kernighan, he recalled, was settling into his new office when a stranger said: “Hey, I’m Dick, let’s go for lunch.” Only later did he realise it was the great Richard Hamming. Kernighan’s verdict: geography is destiny. {032-S02}
Varma’s point was not performative office attendance. “The real creativity happens is in the watercooler conversations,” he said. “It’s in the beer after the office work.”
Ajay Shah credited the post-war American mood: boundless optimism, a flowering of freedom, and little acceptance of top-down authority on either side.
~ Shah also praised Varma’s reading for the episode: “This boy is not a Bengali dreamer.”

quote.text: This is a broad field we are in. Many things are possible. Design the future.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: C is for Unix
sections.caption: how C and the universities spread Unix
body: After Unix booted, Ajay Shah said, came the story of C. Every operating system of the age was written in assembly language, which took someone like Ken Thompson.
Dennis Ritchie asked whether Unix could be written in a high-level language. None was good enough, so he and others built a new one. {032-S07}
“And C was written to make it possible to write Unix in C,” Shah said. Rewritten, Unix could move to more and more machines.
## Antitrust to the rescue

AT&T could have launched its own computers and become a monopoly in computing too. Shah’s opinion is that its battles with antitrust authorities stopped it. {032-S08} It sent Unix to universities instead, under a licence to read and tinker but not commercialise.
A famous book printed the kernel with a line-by-line commentary. At Berkeley, Bill Joy connected Unix to networking, and it carried TCP/IP and the internet.

Steve Jobs chose BSD Unix at NeXT and brought the NeXT team back to Apple. He had relied on advisers he trusted, Shah said, until iTunes was written in roughly a week: “Steve Jobs is said to have got religion.” {032-S10}
~ There are grumblers, Shah said, who say Unix is holding us back, and he has no doubt that the next generation must be found.

quote.text: I want to claim some credit for the economists here.

portraits.hint: American computer scientist, creator of C

sections.label: The philosophy
sections.head: Beauty is a working part
sections.caption: simplicity, small tools and prose
body: Why did Unix win? Ajay Shah began with an aesthetic sense of simplicity. He quoted the computer scientist David Gelernter: “When faced with complexity, our only defence is beauty.” {032-J14}

His second principle was to build one small tool at a time, limited but bulletproof, and let people combine tools like Lego blocks, rather than run one giant top-down project. His own method is to think long with a problem “uploaded” in his brain, then solve the hardest pieces first. {032-C09}
## Prose and code

Third came writing. Bell Labs wrote terse, precise man pages and slim books, and its people improved each other’s drafts. “Writing code is like writing prose,” Shah said. “They’re not different.” {032-C10}
Amit Varma added Deirdre McCloskey, for whom writing is part of research, and Joan Didion: “I don’t know what I think till I write it down.” {032-J15}
Shah questioned anyone who shelves culture and philosophy apart from engineering. In India’s doctor-engineer world, he said, the separation has cost engineers their sense of good engineering.

~ Following Donald Knuth, he said, code should explain the algorithm to a person sitting beside you. Badly written code is thrown away within a year; the Unix community is tending “a garden with fifty-year-old trees”.

quote.text: It’s good to find the hardest things and solve them and get them done.

sections.label: The commons
sections.head: Science by another name
sections.caption: open source and public goods
body: At Bell Labs, Ajay Shah said, sharing code came naturally. It was the culture of science and mathematics: if I prove a theorem, I show you the proof. {032-C13}
The open source movement, he said, is just the continuation of a story that began five hundred years ago, when Newton published his proofs and demonstrations.

In the mid-1970s, by Shah’s account, Bill Gates wrote a manifesto for secret commercial software and Richard Stallman a rival one for software as open as mathematics and physics. At one point, he thought, Microsoft made 90 per cent of all the computer companies’ profits. {#microsoft} Yet it never developed a new idea.
## A real public good

Downloaded code is non-rival and non-excludable, Shah argued: a public good. The US Department of Defense funded TCP/IP and AT&T paid the early salaries, but no government controls Unix or the internet. {032-C14}

Amit Varma saw markets in the broad sense: voluntary cooperation. One of Shah’s closing picks, Eric Raymond’s essay *The Cathedral & the Bazaar*, asks how unpaid volunteers build such software: “It’s like you’re not paying, but they’re building the world’s best software.” {032-R09}
~ And for the Indian nationalists, Shah added: “Nobody called it America Stack, they just called it Unix and the Internet.” {032-J06}

quote.text: I think Unix and the internet are digital public goods. There’s no government in the picture.

sections.label: The freedom
sections.head: Four rupees an email
sections.caption: freedom wired into the internet
body: An operating system can easily exert draconian control, Ajay Shah said, and computing could have become a straitjacket. Unix and the internet instead accepted a great deal of anarchism: anonymous use, encryption, VPNs. {032-C16}

Picture the alternative, he said: a WhatsApp uncle demanding a UID iris scan every time you switch on your phone, “because otherwise terrorists will use phones”, and four rupees charged for each email. {032-J05}
Spam is the price of open email, Shah conceded. It is still better, he said, than claustrophobic control.
## Stubborn frugality
Decades of clever people on underpowered machines have sharpened Unix’s algorithms, he said, so it does more with less hardware, and old computers headed for the bin can be revived. {032-C15}
Amit Varma asked what a normal person could do. Shah asked for practicality: “show me where is the beef, or show me where is the rasgulla?” Varma ruled that anti-national and unhealthy. {032-J02}
~ Shah’s answer: watch, and join, the Linux kernel’s open development through Git, and play with a Raspberry Pi, a credit card-sized computer costing a few thousand rupees. {#raspberry}

quote.text: The internet is deeply wired for free, flexible, anonymous use.

sections.label: The screencast
sections.head: Pipe dreams
sections.caption: the Unix command line
body: In his screencast, Ajay Shah set graphical applications like LibreOffice and Chrome aside. They run on any Unix machine, he said, but the interesting work happens at the command line.

He walked through his directory for the show, with a README to guide his future self, then sorted a table of 23 episodes by length. The shortest ran 46 minutes; Ukraine, at 91, was the longest. {#ukraine}
The pipe joins commands: the output of sort goes to tail, which keeps the last three lines. Data stays in plain text, never in a format only one program can read. {032-C19}
## One line, one insight

With awk, Shah worked out minutes per viewer. In June 2023, about 300 hours went to 1,947 unique viewers, nine minutes each, mostly curious spectators. By November, some 14,000 viewers averaged about 45 minutes. {032-S13}
The early information problem had receded, he thought: people now knew what the show was, and kept coming back.
~ He also wrapped Pandoc, a converter from every file format to every other, into a new command of his own, so that Amit Varma, who does not use Emacs, could get Word files.

quote.text: Plain text files are the universal language by which all the programs speak to each other

side.boxText: Amit Varma calls Brian Kernighan’s *UNIX: A History and a Memoir* a must-read. For Ajay Shah, it is the source of origin stories from Ken Thompson’s forged application to his recruitment by telephone. {032-S03}

contQuote.text: So we can just go look at the sausage factory, we can see what is being done by who and how, and then we can start participating and we can start contributing.

p3.title: Tales from the lab
p3.deck: A junked computer, a motel, a patent office and a chess game

stories.start: at that time there was an obsolete computer which was called a PDP seven
stories.end: it was very stripped down, and so they chose the name Unix
stories.caption: Ken Thompson’s three weeks
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a space game became an operating system
stories.head: Junk in, Unix out
body: Bell Labs had been burned by Multics. Its managers, Ajay Shah said, would hire all kinds of crazy people, but they were not going to fund operating systems. You could fool around on your own time; serious resourcing was out.
Ken Thompson, back from the failed project, found an obsolete PDP-7 lying in a corner. It had perhaps 16 or 32 kilobytes of memory, Shah said, and a disk that was too fast for the computer. {#memory}
Thompson wrote a space travel game on it, in which you flew a spacecraft and tried to land on Jupiter. Brian Kernighan, Shah said, writes that he played it and enjoyed it.
Fighting with that disk, Thompson wrote a disk-scheduling algorithm, a file system and a device driver. Then he understood that he was three weeks from an operating system.

His wife and child happened to be going to California to visit his parents. “He planned it as one week to write an editor, one week to write an assembler, one week to write the operating system kernel, in three weeks I’ll be done,” Shah said. {032-S05}
It worked out exactly like that. Unix booted. It was bare and stripped down, and its name was a nod to the failed Multics.
~ Every office, Shah observed, has a supply of rubbish nobody is using, and this story “runs contrary to any declutter manifesto”: you do want to keep your PDP-7s. {032-J03}
stories.why: Junk hardware, no funding and three weeks alone produced Unix. Amit Varma called it dancing with chains: a too-fast disk and a borrowed budget pushed creativity along rather than stopping it. {#chains}
stories.postscript: Thompson, Shah recalled, said the next revolution will start with a space travel game on some defunct Cray-1 supercomputer.

stories.start: some people in Bell Labs tried to reach out to him
stories.end: He said, Very well, I accept. And that's how He joined uh Bell Labs
stories.caption: the call to every motel
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the recruitment of Ken Thompson
stories.head: Every motel in New Jersey
body: Ken Thompson told Bell Labs he would never work for a corporation. He was a researcher and a thinker, Ajay Shah said, and companies were no good.
Bell Labs kept after him and flew him east to give a talk. In the corridor, reading the names on the doors, he thought how amazing it would be to be near these people. {#corridor}
After the talk he drove to a friend’s house, where a printed offer reached him, then on to a motel, still undecided. Bell Labs called him there too. How, he asked, had they found him?
“Well, we’re the telephone company,” came the answer. “We found the phone number of every motel in New Jersey and we made all the calls and we found you.” {032-S04} He accepted.
~ And that, Shah said, is how Thompson joined Bell Labs.
stories.why: Talent pulls in talent. It was the names on the doors, the clustering and network effects, Ajay Shah said, that drew Thompson in; the telephone company’s persistence did the rest.

stories.start: The brain wave was that there was a patent department inside Bell Labs
stories.end: So all these things were built there and that's how Unix happened
stories.caption: the patent-typesetting gambit
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on funding an operating system by stealth
stories.head: Smuggled in as patent software
body: Even after Unix booted, Bell Labs management refused to fund operating systems, Ajay Shah said, because of the money wasted on Multics.

Then the group had a brainwave. Bell Labs was running at about one patent a day, and patent applications needed strict formatting, diagrams and equations. Management was about to pay an outside vendor for a system that typeset patents. {#patent}

The Unix group offered to build one in-house for the same money. What they knew in their minds was that they would write a whole document-processing system, run it on Unix and build Unix out on modern hardware. Management approved. {032-S06}
~ The tools were roff, then nroff, then troff, which embedded commands for italics, boldface and section numbers in raw text. The word “markup” in HTML, Shah said, originates here.
stories.why: When managers will not back the bet you believe in, find a problem they will pay for, one where your bet is the cheapest solution. Unix was built out on a typesetting budget.

stories.start: a story where uh the president of Bell Labs brought a visitor
stories.end: the fun and games of Richard of of Ken Thompson to a visitor outside
stories.caption: Ken Thompson’s chess program
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why play is a good use of a mind
stories.head: Cute, but is it useful?
body: A powerful visitor was touring Bell Labs with its president, Ajay Shah recalled, when Ken Thompson showed him a program that played chess. “Yeah, this is cute,” the visitor said, “but how is it useful?” {#chess}

Thompson had brought dynamic programming to the chess endgame, listing every mating position and working backwards. The idea came from Richard Bellman and Robert Kalaba at the RAND Corporation. Kalaba, Shah said, was his teacher, and his own PhD thesis, on women in Malaysia, rested on dynamic programming.

The president of Bell Labs had an answer: algorithms developed along the way helped schedule phone calls in the Bell system. Management, Shah said, would not fund an operating system, but it never stopped anyone writing one. {032-S11}
~ Amit Varma added that endgames with seven pieces or fewer are now basically solved, using tablebases.

quote.text: building a space travel game and a chess program is actually a good use of the human mind

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, did Bell Labs succeed, given that its budget was not exceptional?
quiz.a: Its culture and management, not its resources: many organisations could fund one today.

quiz.q: Ken Thompson was undecided, staying at a motel. How did Bell Labs track him down?
quiz.a: As the telephone company, it phoned every motel in New Jersey until it found him.

quiz.q: How did Ken Thompson divide the three weeks his family spent visiting his parents in California?
quiz.a: One week each for an editor, an assembler and the operating system kernel.

quiz.q: Which programming language did Dennis Ritchie and others create, and why?
quiz.a: C, to make it possible to write Unix in a high-level language.

quiz.q: What made Steve Jobs, by Ajay Shah’s account, finally get religion about Unix?
quiz.a: iTunes was written in roughly a week on Apple’s new Unix environment.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s one-line awk program reveal about viewers of the show?
quiz.a: Minutes per unique viewer rose from nine in June to about 45 by November.
